original_title: Nigeria: Borno, Adamawa, and Yobe (BAY) states - Quarter 2 Situation Report, April - June 2026
title: Nigeria: Borno, Adamawa, and Yobe (BAY) states - Quarter 2 Situation Report, April - June 2026
original_summary:
Countries: Nigeria, Cameroon
Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

Please refer to the attached file.

This report is produced by OCHA Nigeria in collaboration with humanitarian partners. It covers the April-June 2026 period. The next report will be issued in October 2026.

Highlights

  • Lean season takes hold with 6.4 million people food insecure across Borno, Adamawa and Yobe states
  • Record Nigeria Humanitarian Fund (NHF) allocation gets underway in northeast, northwest and northcentral Nigeria.
  • As cholera cases rise across Borno, humanitarian partners scale-up life-saving responses
  • Borno State progresses with plans to close IDP camps
  • Escalating insecurity disrupts lives and humanitarian operations across the northeast
  • Nigeria on its way to locally- led and financed humanitarian coordination

Situation overview

Lean season hits northeast communities, driving rising food insecurity.

More than 6.4 million people in Borno, Adamawa and Yobe (BAY) states are projected to face crisis-level hunger or worse during the June–August 2026 lean season, marking the worst acute food insecurity peak recorded in northeast Nigeria in more than a decade.

According to the latest Cadre Harmonisé (CH) food security analysis, conducted jointly by the Government and humanitarian partners, nearly 4 in every 10 people in the BAY states - about 36 per cent of the population - are expected to experience acute food insecurity during the season. The latest projection represents a 10 per cent increase from previously estimates made in October 2025, highlighting the rapid deterioration of food security conditions across the region.

The situation is particularly alarming for the most vulnerable households. More than 1.1 million people are projected to face Emergency (Phase 4) levels of food insecurity, characterized by severe food consumption gaps and heightened risks of acute malnutrition. At the same time, about 10,300 people could fall into Catastrophe (Phase 5), the most extreme level of food insecurity, by August 2026 if urgent action is not taken.

The CH warns that a combination of conflict, economic hardship and climate-related shocks is driving the crisis. Persistent insecurity continues to limit access to farmland and markets, undermining livelihoods and reducing food production. Renewed attacks in parts of Borno State, including Askira/Uba, Chibok, Gwoza and Kaga local government areas, have further restricted agricultural activities and access to essential services.

At the same time, families are grappling with soaring food prices, elevated fuel costs and expensive agricultural inputs as a result of the conflict in the Middle East. Inflation, currency depreciation and rising transportation costs have reduced household purchasing power, making it increasingly difficult for vulnerable communities to meet their basic food needs.

Climate risks are complicating the food security landscape. Early warning information points to the likelihood of localized El Niño-related impacts, including both dry spells and flooding during the current agricultural season. Such shocks could destroy crops, disrupt farming activities and further erode household food stocks and incomes, particularly among already vulnerable rural communities.

Humanitarian agencies say assistance remains a critical lifeline, but current resources are insufficient to match rising needs. As of May 2026, approximately 700,000 people targeted for food assistance under the 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan had not received support, while 830,000 people missed out on planned emergency agricultural assistance because of funding shortfalls.

The Food Security Sector needs US$224.4 million in 2026 to provide food assistance to 1.5 million people and emergency agricultural support to 900,000 people. However, funding remains critically low. As of mid-year, the sector had received only US$76 million, representing only a third of requirements, leaving a funding gap of approximately 66 per cent (US$148.4 million). The shortfall is particularly concerning for agricultural interventions which are critical to helping vulnerable households produce food, protect livelihoods, and reduce dependence on humanitarian assistance.

Without urgent action during the lean season, aid agencies warn that worsening food insecurity could lead to increased displacement, deeper poverty, heightened malnutrition and greater instability across north-east Nigeria. Every day of delay increases the risk of irreversible harm for families already struggling to survive. Additional and rapid funding is urgently needed to expand lifesaving food assistance, support food production and reach the most vulnerable people before hunger escalates further across Borno, Adamawa and Yobe states.
